name: The Ancient Douglas Firs of Indian Canyon
age_estimate: around 400 years (arborist estimate for the largest of the three)

location.address: Indian Canyon Park, on the cliff edge overlooking Mystic Falls, near Chief Spokane Garry's last campsite; trailhead at approximately 4812 W. Canyon Drive, Spokane

access: Free, public city park with hiking trails (part of the larger Palisades Park area, per spokanehistorical.org, which independently confirms the park is public, 155.7 acres, with trails)
transport: West Spokane, Indian Canyon trailhead off W. Canyon Drive; car recommended, some city bus service to the West Hills area
story:
These firs are still standing because they were not worth cutting down. A Douglas fir whose trunk tapers sharply makes poor lumber, and the crews who took nearly all the old growth out of the hills around Spokane walked past three of them on the cliff edge above Mystic Falls.

The largest is around 400 years old. That figure comes from Jeff Perry, the City of Spokane's lead arborist, who told the Spokesman-Review in 2019 that he could get his arms around perhaps a third of the trunk, and that measuring it properly is not really possible, because the tree's roots are holding the edge of the cliff together. That is the best description of it anyone has written. It is not so much standing on the canyon rim as being the canyon rim.

Four centuries puts their germination in the early 1600s. Chief Spokane Garry's last campsite is a short walk from where they stand; he died in 1892, by which time these three were already more than two centuries old.

One caution. All of this rests on a single newspaper feature, although a named city arborist with his arms around the trunk is better evidence than most trees get. No girth has ever been published, and the pin marks the trailhead rather than the trees.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by where they stand: three Douglas firs together right on the cliff edge above Mystic Falls, the largest of them wide enough that a grown man's arms reach only about a third of the way round.

name: The State Champion White Willow of Finch Arboretum

location.address: John A. Finch Arboretum, Spokane, Washington

transport: West Spokane, off Sunset Highway; car or city bus
story:
The largest white willow in Washington started life as somebody's garden tree. A woman came to the Spokane parks department to tell them so: her family planted it more than ninety years ago, when the ground that is now the John A. Finch Arboretum was still houses rather than trees.

The houses went. The willow stayed, and it is now the state champion of its species, the biggest known white willow in Washington, on the word of Jeff Perry, the city's lead arborist.

It is also on borrowed time, and the city says so plainly. In 2019 Perry gave it roughly thirty more years before it starts to split and come down, which is how large willows usually go: not in one storm but in pieces, over years. That is the bargain with the species. White willow grows fast and soft and generous, puts on size quickly and does not do centuries the way an oak does, so a willow of championship size is a rarer thing to stand in front of than ninety years makes it sound.

Its history rests on one newspaper feature and one family's memory, which is thinner than most trees here carry. If you know who planted it, or anything about the houses that used to stand here, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, long and narrow and silver underneath, so the whole crown goes pale when the wind turns them over. It is the largest willow in the arboretum, and the largest of its kind in the state.

name: The First Dawn Redwoods of Finch Arboretum

location.address: John A. Finch Arboretum, Spokane, Washington

transport: West Spokane, off Sunset Highway; car or city bus
story:
Botanists knew this tree from fossils before they knew it was alive. Metasequoia was described from imprints in rock, and everyone assumed that was the end of it, until a living stand turned up in a valley in central China in 1943. A species filed under extinct was still quietly growing.

Seed went out to institutions around the world, and in the 1950s the John A. Finch Arboretum received three of the first dawn redwoods brought to North America. Two are still standing. At about seventy-five years old they are infants by redwood standards, and they are also most of the species' history on this continent.

What makes them worth the walk is visible without knowing any of it. Dawn redwood is a deciduous conifer, which is close to a contradiction: soft feathery needles all summer, rust orange in late autumn, then bare all winter while every evergreen around it carries on as normal. The trunks flute deeply as they age, with vertical channels running down between the branches.

The arboretum is free and sits in west Spokane. These two stand a short walk from the state champion willow, so it is one afternoon rather than two trips. Nobody has recorded a girth for either of them; if you have a tape measure, we would take the number.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them in late autumn, when their needles turn rust orange and fall while the pines and firs around them stay green. In summer, look for soft feathery foliage on straight trunks deeply grooved between the branches.

best_time.label: late October into November, when two conifers in an arboretum of evergreens turn rust orange and go bare

name: The Chestnut Champion
species: Horse Chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), likely the double-flowered cultivar 'Baumannii'

location.address: Edwidge Woldson Park (formerly Pioneer Park), near the Corbin Art Center, 507 W 7th Avenue, Spokane, WA 99204
location.neighbourhood: South Hill (Moore-Turner Heritage Gardens / Corbin Art Center area)

verified_sources: https://www.historicspokane.org/spokane-heritage-trees (Spokane Heritage Tree Register; individual record and tree-level coordinate pulled from the city's own ArcGIS layer, CityandCountyHistoricProp/FeatureServer/1, embedded at historicspokane.org/map, feature 'The Chestnut Champion')
https://www.historylink.org/File/10030 (Laura Arksey, 'Spokane's Champion and Historic Trees', HistoryLink.org Essay 10030, 2012, citing Dr. Edward Lester's tree survey)
access: Free, public city park (Edwidge Woldson Park). A Spokesman-Review caption (seen only as an unfetchable WebSearch snippet, spokesman.com/galleries/2019/may/07/spokanes-most-unique-and-historic-trees/, 403 to both curl and WebFetch) describes it as standing 'in front of the Corbin Arts Center', which reads as the open park rather than the fenced Moore-Turner Heritage Gardens next door. Those Gardens keep seasonal hours (May 16 to September 15, Tuesday to Sunday, 9am to 3:30pm, closed Mondays, per my.spokanecity.org/parks/gardens/moore-turner/); this tree's exact position relative to that fence line is not independently confirmed, so treat the seasonal note as a caveat rather than a certainty.
transport: South Hill, near W 7th Avenue and S Stevens Street; car recommended, city bus service runs along 7th Avenue
how_to_recognise: Look for a large, gnarled horse chestnut near the Corbin Art Center building in Edwidge Woldson Park. If it is the Baumannii cultivar, it flowers heavily in spring but sets no nuts, unlike an ordinary horse chestnut.
story:
Spokane opened a heritage tree register in 1998, and by 2012 it held exactly three trees. All three stand in the same small park on the South Hill, and this is the largest of them: a horse chestnut the city records at 102 feet tall with a crown just as wide.

Take the figure with some caution. A mature horse chestnut usually stops between 50 and 80 feet, so 102 is either a genuinely exceptional tree or a generous measurement, and the register's own wording calls it a contender for state champion size rather than the champion.

The identification splits as well, and that one you can settle yourself on the ground. The city lists it plainly as Aesculus hippocastanum. The 2012 survey by the Spokane tree collector Edward Lester, written up by HistoryLink, has it as the double-flowered cultivar Baumannii, believed to be the largest or second largest in Washington. Baumannii carries sterile double flowers, which means a spring of heavy white candles and then no conkers at all underneath it in autumn.

It grows on ground that belonged to D.C. Corbin, who built railroads into the Inland Northwest and a house on the hill to go with them. The house is the Corbin Art Center now. The apricot behind it and the elm in the gardens next door are the other two trees on that 2012 list, so all three are one short walk.

best_time.label: May, when the white flower candles stand up across the crown

name: Corbin's Apricot

location.address: Edwidge Woldson Park (formerly Pioneer Park), directly behind the former D.C. Corbin House (now the Corbin Art Center), 507 W 7th Avenue, Spokane, WA 99204

verified_sources: https://www.historicspokane.org/spokane-heritage-trees (Spokane Heritage Tree Register; individual record and tree-level coordinate from the city's own ArcGIS layer, CityandCountyHistoricProp/FeatureServer/1, feature 'Corbin's Apricot')
https://www.historylink.org/File/10030 (Laura Arksey, 'Spokane's Champion and Historic Trees', HistoryLink.org Essay 10030, 2012)
access: Free, public city park (Edwidge Woldson Park), on the grounds around the Corbin Art Center building. Its exact position relative to the fenced, seasonal-hours Moore-Turner Heritage Gardens next door (open May 16 to September 15, Tuesday to Sunday, 9am to 3:30pm, closed Mondays) is not independently confirmed; the register's own description places it 'directly behind the house above the rock wall', which reads as the open grounds rather than the gated gardens.
transport: South Hill, near W 7th Avenue and S Stevens Street; car recommended, city bus service runs along 7th Avenue
how_to_recognise: An apricot tree on the grounds behind the Corbin Art Center building, a remnant of the pioneer-era kitchen garden that once stood there, distinguishable from ornamental plantings nearby by its fruit in summer.
story:
Spokane put three trees on its heritage register, and one of them came out of somebody's kitchen garden. Former residents of the D.C. Corbin House remembered a working garden directly behind the building, above the rock wall. Everything else about it is gone. The apricot is the remnant, and the city's register says so in as many words.

A 2012 survey called it a hundred years old, which puts it somewhere around 110 to 115 now, with the usual slack that a round number carries. Prunus armeniaca, the Armenian plum, is not a species that does centuries: commercial orchards pull apricots out and replant long before a tree gets near one. This one was never pulled out, because the garden around it stopped being a garden and became a public park.

D.C. Corbin built railroads into the Inland Northwest and a mansion on the South Hill to go with them. The mansion is the Corbin Art Center now, the grounds are open to anybody, and the tree that once supplied a kitchen is still fruiting on them.

It is history rather than spectacle: a modest fruit tree with a documented job, standing a couple of minutes from the other two trees on that register, a champion-sized horse chestnut and an elm in the restored gardens next door. Nobody has recorded a girth. If you have a tape measure, we would take the number.

name: The Moore-Turner Elm
species: Elm (the city register lists American Elm, Ulmus americana; a 2012 tree survey citing dendrologist Robert Van Pelt identifies the same tree instead as a European/Russian White Elm, Ulmus laevis, and calls it the third-largest of that species in the state; sources disagree and neither has been resolved)

location.address: Moore-Turner Heritage Gardens, Edwidge Woldson Park (formerly Pioneer Park), 507 W 7th Avenue, Spokane, WA 99204

verified_sources: https://www.historicspokane.org/spokane-heritage-trees (Spokane Heritage Tree Register; individual record and tree-level coordinate from the city's own ArcGIS layer, CityandCountyHistoricProp/FeatureServer/1, feature 'The Moore-Turner Elm')

https://www.historylink.org/File/10030 (Laura Arksey, 'Spokane's Champion and Historic Trees', HistoryLink.org Essay 10030, 2012, citing Robert Van Pelt, author of 'Champion Trees of Washington State' and the national Big Tree Program's state coordinator)
access: Free, but within the Moore-Turner Heritage Gardens proper (per the register: 'Located in the historic Moore-Turner Garden'), which keep seasonal hours: open May 16 to September 15, Tuesday to Sunday, 9am to 3:30pm; closed Mondays and outside that season (my.spokanecity.org/parks/gardens/moore-turner/). Say this plainly on the page rather than presenting it as open at any time.
transport: South Hill, near W 7th Avenue and S Stevens Street; car recommended, city bus service runs along 7th Avenue
how_to_recognise: The one large elm within the Moore-Turner Heritage Gardens terraces, in a garden otherwise planted with roses, perennials and a tea house rather than shade trees.
story:
Two credible people have looked at this elm and come back with different species. The City of Spokane's heritage register calls it an American elm, Ulmus americana, 88 feet tall with a 44 foot crown. The 2012 survey published by HistoryLink, citing Robert Van Pelt, who wrote Champion Trees of Washington State and coordinated the national big tree programme here, calls the registered elm in these gardens a European or Russian white elm, Ulmus laevis, and ranks it third largest of that species in the state. Both accounts point at the same tree in the same garden. Nobody has settled it.

The disagreement matters less standing under it than it looks in print, because either answer is a reason to go. A large American elm is a survivor, since Dutch elm disease took most of the big ones across North America inside a generation. A state-ranked white elm is rarer still, a Eurasian species almost nobody here plants.

The garden was laid out from the 1890s by Frank Rockwood Moore and the United States senator George Turner, left to go wild for decades, and dug back out as the Moore-Turner Heritage Gardens. The elm is the one big tree among terraces given over to roses, perennials and a tea house.

Check the calendar first. The gardens open 16 May to 15 September, Tuesday to Sunday, 9am to 3:30pm, and are locked the rest of the year.
